## 1. Identification Strategy
Other: “Within-admissions-portfolio” design (conditioning on the complete set of colleges that admitted a student). 

Rationale:
- Colleges observe rich, partly unmeasured traits (motivation, recommendations, essays) that affect both admissions and later earnings. Because multiple independent admissions committees evaluate the same applicant, the vector of admissions outcomes is an informative sufficient statistic for these unobservables.
- Conditioning on the full offer set (the distribution of selectivity among admitted schools, plus the number of rejections) absorbs most selection on unobservables observed by admissions officers. Variation in the selectivity of the college actually attended, conditional on an identical or near-identical offer set, is then plausibly driven by factors such as financial aid differences, distance, preferences, and idiosyncrasies orthogonal to long-run earnings potential.
- This strategy lets us estimate (i) the marginal effect of attending a more selective college on earnings and (ii) how that effect varies by family background. We can also estimate the partial role of other college characteristics (e.g., net tuition) separately from peer selectivity by exploiting choices among offers that differ on those dimensions.

Secondary component for net tuition:
- Within-portfolio identification of the effect of attended-college net tuition, controlling for the admissions portfolio and selectivity. Optionally, we can strengthen identification by instrumenting net tuition with leave-one-out measures of institutional aid generosity by need group, although this is an extension (see Threats/Robustness).

## 2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable:
  - Continuous treatment: selectivity of the attended college, proxied by the institution’s average SAT of entering students in 1976 (standardized).
  - Additional college characteristics: attended-college net tuition at entry (and potentially expenditures per student, financial aid generosity, etc., where available).

- Control group / counterfactual:
  - Students with the same (or highly similar) admissions portfolios (i.e., the same distribution of selectivity among admitted schools and similar numbers of rejections across selectivity bins) who chose colleges with different selectivity and/or net tuition.

- Treatment timing / event date:
  - College entry year (1976). Outcome measured in 1995–97 (1995 earnings).

- No running variable / cutoff (not an RDD).

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Conditional random choice among offers:
  - Conditional on the admissions portfolio (distribution of admitted-school selectivity and rejections), observed pre-college covariates (student SAT, high school rank, demographics), and intended/actual major, the student’s choice of which offer to accept is as good as random with respect to potential earnings. Plausibility: High. The multiple-screen nature of admissions means the offer set summarizes unobservables viewed by committees. Within that set, choice is often shaped by price, distance, campus fit, and idiosyncratic preferences that are less clearly tied to latent earnings ability.
- Correct measurement of the admissions portfolio:
  - The reported lists of schools applied to/accepted by are accurate. Plausibility: Reasonable but imperfect; these are survey self-reports. We will test sensitivity to excluding observations with implausible or incomplete lists.
- Common support:
  - Sufficient within-portfolio variation in chosen selectivity and net tuition to identify effects. Plausibility: Supported by wide cross-institution variation (SAT 1,020–1,360; variable net tuition) and the fact many applicants receive multiple offers across selectivity tiers.
- SUTVA:
  - No spillovers across students that depend on where peers enroll, conditional on our controls. Plausibility: Reasonable at the individual level for long-run earnings.
- Selection into full-time, full-year work:
  - Conditional on covariates and the admissions portfolio, selection into the analysis sample (full-time, full-year) is not differentially related to chosen selectivity in a way that biases treatment effects. Plausibility: Uncertain. We will assess with IPW/selection checks.

## 4. Threats to Identification and Responses
1) Nonrandom choice within portfolio correlated with latent earnings traits not fully captured by the offer set (e.g., career orientation that also affects which college a student picks among comparable offers).
- Response:
  - Saturate controls for pre-college observables (SAT, HS rank, parental income, gender, race/ethnicity), intended major (from entry), geography, and high school characteristics if available.
  - Rich portfolio controls: fixed effects for the distribution of selectivity among admitted schools (counts within selectivity bins) and number of rejections; also include summary statistics of applied-to (not just admitted) schools.
  - Sensitivity analyses: Oster bounds on coefficients; Rosenbaum bounds for matched subsamples; restrict to students with offers spanning materially different selectivity bins to enhance quasi-random variation.
  - Placebo outcomes (e.g., pre-college expectations if available) to check balance.

2) Measurement error in the offer set (applied/accepted lists).
- Response:
  - Exclude observations with inconsistent or incomplete reporting; cross-validate with institution records where available.
  - Use coarser portfolio bins (selectivity quintiles/deciles) to reduce sensitivity to small misreports.
  - Instrumental variation for attended net tuition using leave-one-out institutional generosity by need group as a robustness device (helps if mismeasurement in price correlates with choice).

3) Selection into the full-time, full-year worker sample in 1995.
- Response:
  - Reweight by the inverse probability of being a full-time, full-year worker estimated from pre-college covariates and portfolio characteristics.
  - Check robustness on broader samples (e.g., including part-time with appropriate controls) and on the NLS-72 replication sample.

## 5. R Code Outline
Note: This is a working template. Replace file names/variable names with the actual ones. Assumes three CSVs: individual-level (one row per student), application-level (one row per student-college), and college-level.

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(stringi)
library(ModelMetrics)

# 1) Load data
ind <- fread("cb_individual.csv")      # id, earnings95, sat_total, hs_rank_pct, parent_income, gender, race, major, attended_college_id, region, etc.
apps <- fread("cb_applications.csv")   # id, college_id, applied (0/1), admitted (0/1)
coll <- fread("cb_college_chars.csv")  # college_id, avg_sat_1976, net_tuition_1976, expenditures_per_student_1976, etc.

# 2) Prepare college characteristics
coll[, avg_sat_std := scale(avg_sat_1976)]
# Create selectivity bins (quintiles here; can switch to deciles if support allows)
nbins <- 5
sat_cuts <- quantile(coll$avg_sat_1976, probs = seq(0,1,length.out=nbins+1), na.rm=TRUE)
coll[, sat_bin := cut(avg_sat_1976, breaks = sat_cuts, include.lowest = TRUE, labels = FALSE)]

# 3) Merge college info onto applications and attended college
apps <- merge(apps, coll[, .(college_id, avg_sat_1976, avg_sat_std, sat_bin)], by="college_id", all.x=TRUE)
ind  <- merge(ind, coll[, .(college_id, avg_sat_1976, avg_sat_std, net_tuition_1976,
                            expenditures_per_student_1976, sat_bin)],
              by.x="attended_college_id", by.y="college_id", all.x=TRUE, suffixes=c("", "_attend"))

setnames(ind, c("avg_sat_std_attend","avg_sat_1976_attend","sat_bin_attend"),
         c("attend_sat_std","attend_sat","attend_sat_bin"))
setnames(ind, c("net_tuition_1976","expenditures_per_student_1976"),
         c("attend_net_tuition","attend_expenditures"))

# 4) Construct admissions portfolio features at the student level
# Counts of ADMITTED offers by selectivity bin; likewise for APPLIED and REJECTED
apps[, rejected := as.integer(applied==1 & admitted==0)]

port_admit <- dcast(apps[admitted==1], id ~ paste0("admit_bin", sat_bin), fun.aggregate=length, value.var="sat_bin")
port_apply <- dcast(apps[applied==1],  id ~ paste0("apply_bin", sat_bin), fun.aggregate=length, value.var="sat_bin")
port_rej   <- dcast(apps[rejected==1], id ~ paste0("rej_bin",   sat_bin), fun.aggregate=length, value.var="sat_bin")

# Fill missing with zeros
for(dt in list(port_admit, port_apply, port_rej)) {
  missing_cols <- setdiff(paste0(rep(c("admit_bin","apply_bin","rej_bin"), each=nbins),
                                 rep(1:nbins, times=3)),
                          names(dt))
  if(length(missing_cols)>0) dt[, (missing_cols) := 0L]
}

portfolio <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y,by="id",all=TRUE), list(port_admit, port_apply, port_rej))
for(v in setdiff(names(portfolio), "id")) portfolio[is.na(get(v)), (v) := 0L]

# Create compact portfolio ID (string) based on admitted and rejected counts by bin
# You can include applied counts too if desired
portfolio[, portfolio_id := do.call(paste, c(.SD, sep="_")),
          .SDcols = grep("^(admit_bin|rej_bin)\\d+$", names(portfolio), value=TRUE)]

# Also compute summary stats of admitted schools' selectivity (mean, max)
admit_summ <- apps[admitted==1,
                   .(admit_mean_sat = mean(avg_sat_1976, na.rm=TRUE),
                     admit_max_sat  = max(avg_sat_1976,  na.rm=TRUE),
                     n_admits = .N),
                   by=.(id)]
admit_summ[, `:=`(admit_mean_sat_std = as.numeric(scale(admit_mean_sat)),
                  admit_max_sat_std  = as.numeric(scale(admit_max_sat)))]

# 5) Merge portfolios and summaries into individual file
ind <- merge(ind, portfolio[, .(id, portfolio_id)], by="id", all.x=TRUE)
ind <- merge(ind, admit_summ, by="id", all.x=TRUE)

# 6) Analysis sample restrictions
# Keep full-time, full-year workers if indicated by a binary flag; here assume 'ftfy_1995' exists
ind <- ind[ftfy_1995==1 & !is.na(earnings95) & !is.na(attend_sat_std) & !is.na(portfolio_id)]

# 7) Covariates and transformations
ind[, ln_earn := log(earnings95)]
# Parental income quartiles
ind[, parent_inc_q := cut(parent_income, breaks=quantile(parent_income, probs=seq(0,1,0.25), na.rm=TRUE),
                          include.lowest=TRUE, labels=FALSE)]
# Standardize student SAT and HS rank
ind[, sat_std    := as.numeric(scale(sat_total))]
ind[, hs_rank_std:= as.numeric(scale(hs_rank_pct))]  # sign as appropriate

# 8) Main specification: within-portfolio FE
# Identify portfolios with at least 2 students to avoid singleton FE
port_counts <- ind[, .N, by=portfolio_id][N>=2]
est_dat <- ind[portfolio_id %in% port_counts$portfolio_id]

# Include interactions with parental background for heterogeneity
est_main <- feols(
  ln_earn ~ attend_sat_std * i(parent_inc_q) + attend_net_tuition + sat_std + hs_rank_std +
    i(major) + i(gender) + i(race) + i(region) + n_admits + admit_mean_sat_std + admit_max_sat_std,
  data = est_dat,
  fixef = ~ portfolio_id,
  cluster = ~ attended_college_id + portfolio_id
)

summary(est_main)

# 9) Robustness check 1: Restrict to students with strongly varied options
# Keep only those with at least one admit in top 2 bins and one in bottom 2 bins
# Build counts by bin from port_admit merged back
admit_bins <- merge(ind[, .(id)], port_admit, by="id", all.x=TRUE)
for(v in setdiff(names(admit_bins),"id")) admit_bins[is.na(get(v)), (v):=0L]
admit_bins[, top2 := get(paste0("admit_bin", nbins)) + get(paste0("admit_bin", nbins-1))]
admit_bins[, bot2 := get("admit_bin1") + get("admit_bin2")]
strong_choice <- admit_bins[top2>=1 & bot2>=1, id]

est_dat_rc <- est_dat[id %in% strong_choice]

est_rb1 <- feols(
  ln_earn ~ attend_sat_std * i(parent_inc_q) + attend_net_tuition + sat_std + hs_rank_std +
    i(major) + i(gender) + i(race) + i(region) + n_admits + admit_mean_sat_std + admit_max_sat_std,
  data = est_dat_rc,
  fixef = ~ portfolio_id,
  cluster = ~ attended_college_id + portfolio_id
)
summary(est_rb1)

# 10) Optional robustness check 2: Inverse probability weights for selection into FTFY
# Estimate propensity of FTFY using pre-college and portfolio variables on the full C&B sample
# (Illustrative; requires the full sample with ftfy_1995 available for all)
# full_ind <- fread("cb_individual.csv")
# full_ind <- merge(full_ind, portfolio[, .(id, portfolio_id)], by="id", all.x=TRUE)
# full_ind <- merge(full_ind, admit_summ, by="id", all.x=TRUE)
# ps_mod <- glm(ftfy_1995 ~ sat_std + hs_rank_std + i(gender) + i(race) + i(region) +
#                 n_admits + admit_mean_sat_std + admit_max_sat_std,
#               data=full_ind, family=binomial())
# ind$ipw <- 1 / pmax(pmin(predict(ps_mod, newdata=ind, type="response"), 0.99), 0.01)
# est_ipw <- feols(
#   ln_earn ~ attend_sat_std * i(parent_inc_q) + attend_net_tuition + sat_std + hs_rank_std +
#     i(major) + i(gender) + i(race) + i(region) + n_admits + admit_mean_sat_std + admit_max_sat_std,
#   data = est_dat, fixef = ~ portfolio_id, cluster = ~ attended_college_id + portfolio_id, weights = ~ ipw
# )
# summary(est_ipw)
```

Notes:
- The core identification comes from the portfolio fixed effects. We also add continuous portfolio summaries (mean/max admitted SAT, number of admits) to absorb residual differences if portfolio bins are imperfect.
- You can replace quintiles with deciles if support is adequate; that tightens the portfolio controls.
- The net tuition coefficient is identified from within-portfolio choices across colleges with different tuition levels; if you wish to instrument attended net tuition, construct a leave-one-out “aid generosity by need group” instrument at the college level and use iv_robust estimators (e.g., fixest’s feols with iv or ivreg).

## 6. Expected Results
- Direction: Small average payoff of attending a more selective college once conditioning on the admissions portfolio—close to zero to modestly positive. I expect the average effect of a 1 SD increase in attended-college selectivity to be roughly 0–3% higher earnings by 1995 for this cohort.
- Heterogeneity: Larger positive effects for students from lower parental income backgrounds (5–8% per 1 SD), reflecting stronger returns to networks, signaling, and resource access. Weaker or null effects for higher-income backgrounds.
- Net tuition: Conditional on selectivity and portfolio, I expect little independent effect of higher net tuition on earnings (tuition largely prices quality already captured by selectivity/resources), though higher institutional expenditures per student may correlate positively with earnings.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
- C1: Conditioning set captures unobserved ability seen by admissions committees (via detailed admissions portfolio controls). Score: 1
- C2: Sufficient within-portfolio variation in chosen selectivity/net tuition to identify effects. Score: 1
- C3: Accurate measurement of the admissions portfolio (applied/accepted lists). Score: 0 (self-reported; some misclassification risk)
- C4: Sample selection into full-time, full-year does not differentially bias estimates after controls/weights. Score: 0 (uncertain; addressed with IPW robustness)
- C5: Model specification and overlap (support) are appropriate; robustness shows stability across specifications and restrictions. Score: 1

Overall, the design leverages a powerful feature of the setting—multiple independent admissions screens—to mitigate selection on unobservables and identify the causal effect of college selectivity, with informative heterogeneity by family background and a way to assess the incremental role of other college characteristics like net tuition.
